cues.text: Let's turn now to intent-based networking, often shortened to I B N.
The central idea is this.
Traditionally, an engineer tells each device exactly what to do, one low-level command at a time.
Intent-based networking changes the starting point.
Instead of individual low-level commands, you express the desired outcome, the result you want the network to deliver, and the system works out how to achieve it.
Now, how does that work in practice?
The source describes a sequence of stages, and the order matters.
First, translate the intent into policy and configuration.
Second, activate that policy and configuration on the network.
Third, collect telemetry, which means gathering measurements and state information from the network as it runs.
Fourth, verify the state of the network against the intent, in other words, check whether what the network is actually doing matches what you said you wanted.
And fifth, remediate or alert.
If the network has drifted from the intent, the system either corrects the problem, which is remediation, or raises an alert so that a person can respond.
Notice that this forms a loop.
Telemetry feeds verification, verification triggers remediation or alerts, and the cycle continues.
That is why it is described as a closed loop.
How does this relate to software-defined networking, or S D N?
The source says S D N provides programmability that can enable I B N.
Because S D N lets you control the network through software, it gives intent-based systems a way to push out changes.
But S D N is not the only route.
Intent-based management may also orchestrate traditional equipment, meaning older, conventional devices that are not part of an S D N design can still be managed through an intent-based approach.
There is a caution here too.
For the closed loop to work, it requires four things.
First, accurate models, because the system's picture of the network must match reality.
Second, validation, so that changes are checked before and after they are applied.
Third, policy conflict resolution, because two policies may contradict each other and the system needs a way to decide between them.
And fourth, controlled rollback, which means being able to undo a change in an orderly, managed way if it does not behave as intended.
Let us make this concrete with the example intent from the source.
The intent is: guest users may access the Internet but not payroll, and the examination portal receives sufficient capacity.
Look at what is being said.
It is a statement of outcomes.
Guests get the Internet.
Guests do not get payroll.
And the examination portal gets enough capacity.
Nothing here names a specific device or command.
To make this real, the intent is translated into identity, VLAN and security policy, together with Q o S policy.
Q o S stands for quality of service, the mechanism for giving certain traffic the capacity or priority it needs.
So the identity, VLAN and security part addresses who the guests are and what they can reach, and the Q o S part addresses the capacity for the examination portal.
Next, that policy is deployed to devices.
Then comes verification, and the source is specific: run tests for what should be allowed and tests for what should be denied.
So you check that a guest can reach the Internet, and you check that a guest cannot reach payroll.
Both kinds of test matter.
Finally, you monitor for deviations, watching for any departure from the intent over time.
Now, two important warnings from the source.
First: do not equate natural language intent with automatic correctness.
Just because an intent is written in plain, readable words, and the system accepts it, does not mean the resulting configuration is right.
The translation could be wrong, or the wording could be ambiguous, so it still has to be verified.
Second: policy changes should be staged, reviewed and auditable.
Staged means rolled out in steps rather than all at once.
Reviewed means checked by someone before they take effect.
And auditable means there is a record of what was changed, so that you can trace it afterwards.
